meta.title: Biophysics — general-exam nucleus
meta.note: Explanations authored for Bucket Academy (original prose; equations are facts). Open sources only.

atoms.title: Boltzmann distribution
atoms.summary: At thermal equilibrium, the probability of a state falls off exponentially with its energy.

depths.eli5: Nature prefers low-energy states, but warmth lets it visit higher ones. The hotter it is, the more often costly states get sampled.
depths.core: A system in contact with a heat bath at temperature T occupies state i with probability proportional to the Boltzmann factor e^(-E_i/kT). This single rule underlies essentially every equilibrium argument in biophysics: folding, binding, and transport all reduce to comparing Boltzmann weights.
depths.deep: k_B is Boltzmann's constant; kT (~0.6 kcal/mol at body temperature) is the natural energy scale of biology. Energy differences of a few kT are the difference between 'always' and 'never'.

atoms.note: Memorize kT ≈ 0.6 kcal/mol ≈ 2.5 kJ/mol at 310 K — your unit of biological 'is this significant?'.
atoms.art_prompt: a ladder of discrete energy levels with population dots thinning exponentially toward the top

quiz.prompt: What sets the energy scale that decides whether an energy gap matters in biology, and roughly how big is it at body temperature?
quiz.answer: k_BT — the thermal energy, ≈ 0.6 kcal/mol (2.5 kJ/mol) at 310 K.

quiz.prompt: Two conformations differ by ΔE = 2.4 kcal/mol at 310 K. Roughly what is the population ratio of the higher to the lower state?
quiz.answer: ratio ≈ e^(−ΔE/kT) = e^(−2.4/0.6) = e^(−4) ≈ 0.018, so about 1.8% — the high state is ~55× rarer.

atoms.title: Partition function
atoms.summary: The sum of all Boltzmann factors — the normalizer that turns energies into probabilities and free energies.

depths.eli5: Add up how 'available' every state is. That total tells you everything measurable about the system.
depths.core: Z normalizes the Boltzmann distribution and is the bridge to thermodynamics: once you can write Z, you can extract free energy, average energy, and any observable by differentiation.
depths.deep: For independent subsystems Z factorizes (Z = ∏ z_k), which is why two-state models and binding polynomials are so tractable — you just multiply small partition functions.

atoms.art_prompt: many small energy-level ladders being summed into one master quantity Z

quiz.prompt: Why is the partition function called the 'bridge to thermodynamics'?
quiz.answer: Because every thermodynamic quantity (free energy, average energy, entropy) is obtained from Z or its derivatives.

quiz.prompt: Write the probability of state i in terms of Z, and explain what role Z plays.
quiz.answer: p_i = e^(−E_i/kT)/Z; Z is the normalization constant ensuring the probabilities sum to 1.

atoms.title: Free energy from the partition function
atoms.summary: Free energy is just the log of the partition function — the quantity systems minimize at constant T.

depths.eli5: One number that balances 'low energy' against 'many ways to arrange' — systems settle where it's smallest.
depths.core: The Helmholtz free energy F = −kT ln Z packages energy and entropy together. At constant temperature and volume, equilibrium is the state of minimum F; differences in F drive every spontaneous biomolecular process.
depths.deep: F = U − TS. The entropy term TS is why warm, floppy, high-multiplicity states win even at a small energy cost — the engine behind the hydrophobic effect and chain entropy.

atoms.art_prompt: two pans of a balance labeled energy and entropy, with free energy as the needle

quiz.prompt: What quantity do systems minimize at constant temperature and volume?
quiz.answer: The Helmholtz free energy F = U − TS = −kT ln Z.

quiz.prompt: Why can a process that increases energy still happen spontaneously?
quiz.answer: If it increases entropy enough that TΔS outweighs ΔU, ΔF is still negative — entropy can pay for energy.

atoms.title: Gibbs free energy
atoms.summary: At constant temperature and pressure (the cell's condition), spontaneity is governed by ΔG.

depths.eli5: Will it happen on its own? Compare the heat released to the order lost. ΔG < 0 means yes.
depths.core: Biology runs at constant pressure, so the Gibbs free energy — not the Helmholtz F — is the right potential. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS combines enthalpy (bonds, contacts) and entropy (disorder). Every binding constant and folding equilibrium is a ΔG in disguise.
depths.deep: ΔG° = −RT ln K links the standard free-energy change to the equilibrium constant — the equation you use to convert any measured K_d or K_eq into an energy.

atoms.note: ΔG°' = −RT ln K — the most-used equation in all of biochemistry.
atoms.art_prompt: enthalpy and entropy arrows combining into a single downhill free-energy slope

quiz.prompt: Which free energy governs spontaneity at constant T and P, and what is its formula?
quiz.answer: Gibbs free energy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

quiz.prompt: A binding reaction has K = 10^6 M^-1 at 310 K. Estimate ΔG° (RT ≈ 0.6 kcal/mol).

atoms.title: Eigenvalues & normal modes
atoms.summary: Linear systems decompose into independent modes — directions that simply scale. This is how we read out collective motion.

depths.eli5: Complicated wobbling is really a few simple wobbles stacked up. Find those simple ones and the motion becomes clear.
depths.core: An eigenvector of a matrix is a direction that the matrix only stretches (by its eigenvalue). For a protein's stiffness matrix, the eigenvectors are normal modes — coordinated motions — and the small eigenvalues are the soft, biologically important large-scale motions.
depths.deep: Diagonalizing the Hessian (or the connectivity matrix in network models) turns coupled dynamics into independent oscillators. Low-frequency modes dominate functional conformational change.

atoms.art_prompt: a tangled spring network resolving into a few clean orthogonal vibration arrows

quiz.prompt: In a protein elastic model, what do the eigenvectors of the stiffness matrix represent, and which eigenvalues matter most biologically?
quiz.answer: Eigenvectors are the normal modes (collective motions); the smallest non-zero eigenvalues are the soft, large-scale, functionally important modes.

atoms.title: The hydrophobic effect
atoms.summary: Nonpolar groups cluster in water not because they attract each other, but because water gains entropy when they hide.

depths.eli5: Oil beads up in water because water 'likes' to avoid wrapping around oil. Pushing the oil together frees the water to be messy again.
depths.core: Burying nonpolar surface releases ordered 'cage' water back into the bulk, raising entropy. The driving force is therefore largely entropic (a positive ΔS), which is why it strengthens with temperature over a wide range. It is the dominant force folding proteins and assembling membranes.
depths.deep: Classic signature: a large positive heat-capacity change (ΔCp) on exposing nonpolar surface, and a folding free energy that is a small difference of large enthalpic and entropic terms — making proteins marginally stable (~5–15 kcal/mol).

atoms.note: Marginal stability (only a few kT) is a feature: it lets proteins fold reversibly and be regulated/degraded.
atoms.art_prompt: ordered water cages around two oily blobs releasing into disordered bulk as the blobs merge

quiz.prompt: Is the hydrophobic effect mainly enthalpic or entropic, and whose entropy increases?
quiz.answer: Mainly entropic — the water's entropy increases when ordered cage water around nonpolar surface is released to the bulk.

quiz.prompt: Why is a folded protein only marginally stable (a few kcal/mol)?
quiz.answer: Folding free energy is a small difference between large opposing enthalpic and entropic terms, so the net is small — which usefully keeps folding reversible and regulatable.

atoms.title: Electrostatic screening & the Debye length
atoms.summary: Salt ions cloud around charges and cut off electrostatic interactions beyond the Debye length.

depths.eli5: In salty water, charges get surrounded by opposite ions and stop 'feeling' each other past a short distance.
depths.core: Mobile ions screen charges: a charge's potential decays as e^(−r/λ_D). At physiological salt (~150 mM) λ_D ≈ 0.8 nm, so electrostatics in the cell is short-ranged. This is the linearized Poisson–Boltzmann picture.
depths.deep: λ_D shrinks as 1/√(ionic strength). Experiments that titrate salt are reading out the electrostatic contribution to binding/folding by tuning how far charges 'see'.

atoms.note: λ_D ≈ 0.3 nm / √(I in molar). At 0.1 M, ≈ 1 nm.
atoms.art_prompt: a central charge surrounded by a fading cloud of counter-ions, potential decaying with distance

quiz.prompt: What physically causes the Debye length, and how does it change with salt concentration?
quiz.answer: Mobile counter-ions screen charges; λ_D decreases as ionic strength increases (∝ 1/√I).

quiz.prompt: Roughly what is the Debye length at physiological ionic strength, and what does that imply about electrostatics in the cell?
quiz.answer: ≈ 0.8–1 nm, so electrostatic interactions are effectively short-ranged inside cells.

atoms.title: Protein structure hierarchy
atoms.summary: Sequence (primary) → local helices/sheets (secondary) → 3D fold (tertiary) → assemblies (quaternary).

depths.eli5: A protein is a bead string that coils into local shapes, folds into a blob, and sometimes teams up with other blobs.
depths.core: Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence; secondary structure is local backbone motifs (α-helix, β-sheet) stabilized by hydrogen bonds; tertiary is the full 3D fold; quaternary is multi-chain assembly. Function lives in the tertiary/quaternary level.
depths.deep: The α-helix and β-sheet were predicted from H-bonding geometry before being seen — a landmark of structural reasoning. Backbone dihedral angles (φ, ψ) parameterize secondary structure (see Ramachandran).

atoms.art_prompt: four panels: bead string, a helix and sheet, a folded domain, a multi-subunit complex

quiz.prompt: Name the four levels of protein structure in order.
quiz.answer: Primary (sequence) → secondary (helices/sheets) → tertiary (3D fold) → quaternary (multi-chain assembly).

quiz.prompt: What interaction primarily stabilizes secondary structure?
quiz.answer: Backbone hydrogen bonds (between C=O and N–H groups).

atoms.title: The Ramachandran plot
atoms.summary: Allowed backbone (φ, ψ) angles cluster into a few regions — and those regions ARE the secondary-structure types.

depths.eli5: Only certain twist combinations of the backbone don't bump atoms together. Those allowed twists make helices and sheets.
depths.core: Steric clashes restrict the two backbone dihedrals φ and ψ to a few regions; the α-helix and β-sheet sit in distinct basins. The plot is the canonical validation tool for structures — outliers signal errors.
depths.deep: Glycine (no side chain) accesses extra regions; proline is restricted. The plot is a direct, geometric consequence of excluded volume — a beautiful example of structure from sterics alone.

atoms.art_prompt: a phi-psi scatter with labeled alpha and beta basins emerging from a clash map

quiz.prompt: What two angles are plotted, and why are only some regions allowed?
quiz.answer: Backbone dihedrals φ and ψ; only some combinations avoid steric clashes between atoms.

quiz.prompt: Why does glycine access regions other residues cannot?
quiz.answer: It has only a hydrogen as its side chain, so it has far less steric restriction.

atoms.title: The ideal polymer chain
atoms.summary: A flexible chain of N random links behaves like a random walk: its size grows as the square root of length.

depths.eli5: A floppy string folded at random doesn't reach far — double its length and it only gets about 1.4× wider.
depths.core: Treating each of N segments (length b) as an independent random step gives a Gaussian coil with end-to-end size R ~ b√N. This is the baseline 'no interactions' model for unfolded proteins and DNA, and the reference against which real chains are compared.
depths.deep: Self-avoidance (excluded volume) swells the coil to R ~ b N^0.59 (Flory); a poor solvent collapses it. Folding is, in part, a dramatic departure from random-coil statistics.

atoms.art_prompt: a random-walk coil with its root-mean-square end-to-end distance marked

quiz.prompt: How does an ideal chain's size scale with the number of segments N?
quiz.answer: As √N (R ~ b√N) — like a random walk.

quiz.prompt: Why does ⟨R²⟩ = Nb² for independent segments? Sketch the reasoning.
quiz.answer: R = Σ b_i; ⟨R²⟩ = Σ⟨b_i·b_j⟩; cross-terms average to zero for independent random directions, leaving N terms of b², so ⟨R²⟩ = Nb².

atoms.title: Worm-like chain & persistence length
atoms.summary: Stiff polymers (like DNA) are characterized by a persistence length — the distance over which the chain 'forgets' its direction.

depths.eli5: Some strings are stiff like cooked spaghetti — they stay straight for a while before bending. That 'while' is the persistence length.
depths.core: The worm-like chain models semiflexible polymers with bending stiffness. The persistence length l_p sets the crossover from rod-like (short pieces) to coil-like (long pieces). DNA's l_p ≈ 50 nm; a disordered protein's is ~0.5–1 nm.
depths.deep: The force–extension of a WLC underlies single-molecule pulling experiments (optical/magnetic tweezers) and lets you read mechanical properties of DNA and proteins one molecule at a time.

atoms.art_prompt: a semiflexible filament straight over one persistence length then curling beyond it

quiz.prompt: Define persistence length in one sentence.
quiz.answer: The contour distance over which a polymer's backbone direction stays correlated (it 'forgets' its orientation beyond it).

quiz.prompt: DNA has l_p ≈ 50 nm. Is a 30 nm fragment more rod-like or coil-like?
quiz.answer: More rod-like, since its length is shorter than the persistence length.

atoms.title: Two-state folding equilibrium
atoms.summary: Many small proteins fold all-or-none: only folded and unfolded states are populated, set by a single ΔG.

depths.eli5: Some proteins are either fully folded or fully unfolded — almost nothing in between — like a switch.
depths.core: In the two-state approximation the equilibrium between folded (F) and unfolded (U) is governed by one free energy, ΔG_fold. Cooperative, sigmoidal melting curves (vs temperature or denaturant) are the experimental signature, and fitting them gives ΔG.
depths.deep: Cooperativity arises because partially folded states are higher in free energy than either end — the funnel makes the intermediate region thermodynamically unfavorable, so the population is bimodal.

atoms.art_prompt: a sigmoidal melting curve with folded and unfolded baskets at the ends

quiz.prompt: What is the experimental signature of two-state folding?
quiz.answer: A cooperative, sigmoidal transition (vs temperature or denaturant) with only folded and unfolded states populated.

quiz.prompt: Express the fraction folded in terms of ΔG_fold.
quiz.answer: f_F = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔG_unfold/kT)) ... equivalently f_F = 1/(1+K) with K = [U]/[F] = e^(−ΔG_fold/kT).

atoms.title: Energy landscape & the folding funnel
atoms.summary: Folding is a biased downhill search on a funnel-shaped landscape, not a single pathway.

depths.eli5: A protein folds by tumbling 'downhill' on a funnel toward its shape — many routes, one bottom.
depths.core: Landscape theory replaced the idea of one folding route with a statistical funnel: many high-energy unfolded conformations narrowing toward the native state. Energetic bias (the funnel's slope) beats the entropy of the search, resolving Levinthal's paradox.
depths.deep: Ruggedness (local minima) can trap intermediates or misfold; the principle of minimal frustration says evolved sequences have smooth-enough funnels to fold reliably.

atoms.art_prompt: a 3D funnel with many trajectories spiraling to a single native minimum

quiz.prompt: What does the funnel picture replace, and what does it resolve?
quiz.answer: It replaces the single-pathway view with a statistical downhill search and resolves Levinthal's paradox.

quiz.prompt: What does 'minimal frustration' mean for an evolved protein sequence?
quiz.answer: Its interactions are mutually compatible enough that the funnel is smooth, so it folds reliably without getting trapped.

atoms.title: Anfinsen's thermodynamic hypothesis
atoms.summary: The native structure is encoded by the sequence alone — it is the global free-energy minimum.

depths.eli5: A protein's shape is written into its sequence; unfold it and it folds right back.
depths.core: Anfinsen showed a denatured enzyme can spontaneously refold to its active form, implying the native state is the thermodynamically most stable structure for that sequence under physiological conditions — the founding principle of structure prediction.
depths.deep: Caveats: chaperones assist kinetics in vivo, and some proteins are kinetically trapped or require co-translational folding — but the thermodynamic hypothesis remains the conceptual basis of the field (and of AlphaFold's premise).

atoms.art_prompt: an enzyme unfolding and spontaneously refolding to the same active shape

quiz.prompt: State Anfinsen's hypothesis in one sentence.
quiz.answer: A protein's native 3D structure is determined by its amino-acid sequence and corresponds to the global free-energy minimum.

quiz.prompt: Name one in vivo caveat to the pure thermodynamic picture.
quiz.answer: Chaperones, kinetic traps, or co-translational folding can matter for getting there, even if the native state is still the stable one.

atoms.title: Mutational stability change (ΔΔG)
atoms.summary: How much a point mutation stabilizes or destabilizes the fold — the workhorse number of protein engineering.

depths.eli5: Change one amino acid: does the protein hold together better or worse? That difference is ΔΔG.
depths.core: ΔΔG compares the folding free energy of a mutant to wild type. Positive (by the destabilizing convention) means the mutation weakens the fold. Predicting ΔΔG from structure is a core design/variant-effect task, and a place where simple physics often rivals machine learning.
depths.deep: ΔΔG for stability is distinct from effects on aggregation or function — a mutation can be stabilizing yet pathogenic (e.g. by promoting aggregation), so matching the right observable to the question matters.

atoms.note: Sign conventions differ between tools — always check which direction 'destabilizing' points.
atoms.art_prompt: wild-type vs mutant folded states on a shifted free-energy scale

quiz.prompt: What does ΔΔG measure?
quiz.answer: The change in folding free energy caused by a mutation (mutant minus wild type).

quiz.prompt: Can a stabilizing mutation still cause disease? Explain.
quiz.answer: Yes — stability and aggregation/function are different observables; a mutation can stabilize the fold yet promote aggregation or impair function.

atoms.title: Binding & the dissociation constant
atoms.summary: K_d is the ligand concentration at which a site is half-occupied — the universal currency of molecular recognition.

depths.eli5: How much ligand do you need before half the proteins are bound? That concentration is K_d. Smaller K_d = tighter binding.
depths.core: From mass action, fractional occupancy follows a hyperbola θ = [L]/(K_d + [L]); at [L] = K_d, θ = 0.5. K_d links directly to energy via ΔG° = RT ln K_d, so a 10× tighter binder is ~1.4 kcal/mol more stable.
depths.deep: K_d = k_off/k_on ties equilibrium to kinetics; many drugs are optimized on k_off (residence time) rather than K_d alone.

atoms.note: nM K_d ≈ tight, µM ≈ moderate, mM ≈ weak. Each 10× in K_d ≈ 1.4 kcal/mol at 310 K.
atoms.art_prompt: a binding hyperbola with the half-saturation point marked at L = Kd

quiz.prompt: What does K_d equal in terms of occupancy?
quiz.answer: The free-ligand concentration at which the binding site is half-occupied (θ = 0.5).

quiz.prompt: Show that occupancy is θ = [L]/(K_d+[L]).
quiz.answer: From K_d = [P][L]/[PL], θ = [PL]/([P]+[PL]) = [L]/(K_d+[L]) after substituting [PL] = [P][L]/K_d.

atoms.title: Cooperativity & the Hill equation
atoms.summary: When binding one ligand helps the next, the binding curve sharpens from a hyperbola into a switch.

depths.eli5: If grabbing one molecule makes it easier to grab more, the protein flips from 'off' to 'on' over a narrow range — like a switch.
depths.core: The Hill coefficient n measures cooperativity: n = 1 is independent sites; n > 1 is positive cooperativity (sigmoidal curve). Hemoglobin's O₂ binding (n ≈ 2.8) is the classic example that makes oxygen delivery efficient.
depths.deep: The Hill equation is a phenomenological limit (infinitely cooperative would give n = number of sites); mechanistic models (MWC, KNF) explain where cooperativity comes from.

atoms.art_prompt: a hyperbola morphing into a steep sigmoid as cooperativity increases

quiz.prompt: What does a Hill coefficient n > 1 indicate?
quiz.answer: Positive cooperativity — binding one ligand increases affinity for the next, giving a sigmoidal (switch-like) curve.

quiz.prompt: Why is cooperative O₂ binding useful for hemoglobin?
quiz.answer: The sigmoidal curve lets it load O₂ in the lungs and unload it in tissues over a small change in O₂ pressure.

atoms.title: MWC allostery
atoms.summary: Cooperativity from a concerted switch between a tense (T) and relaxed (R) state of the whole assembly.

depths.eli5: The whole protein flips together between two shapes; ligands tip the balance toward the one that binds them better.
depths.core: The Monod–Wyman–Changeux model: a symmetric oligomer pre-exists in two states (T, low affinity; R, high affinity) in equilibrium. Ligand binds R better, so binding shifts the population toward R — producing cooperativity without sequential induced fit.
depths.deep: MWC (concerted) vs KNF (sequential) are the two canonical frameworks; real allostery often lies between, and MWC's 'conformational selection' view connects to modern ensemble/energy-landscape thinking.

atoms.art_prompt: a symmetric oligomer toggling concertedly between tense and relaxed states

quiz.prompt: In MWC, where does cooperativity come from?
quiz.answer: From a pre-existing equilibrium between a low-affinity (T) and high-affinity (R) state; ligand binding shifts the whole assembly toward R.

quiz.prompt: How does MWC differ from the KNF (induced-fit) model?
quiz.answer: MWC is concerted (all subunits switch together, conformational selection); KNF is sequential (each binding event induces a local change).

atoms.title: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
atoms.summary: Enzyme rate rises with substrate then saturates; K_M and V_max characterize the enzyme.

depths.eli5: Give an enzyme more substrate and it speeds up — until it's working flat out and can't go faster.
depths.core: Under the steady-state (Briggs–Haldane) assumption for the enzyme–substrate complex, the initial rate is a hyperbola in [S]. K_M is the substrate concentration at half V_max (loosely, an affinity), and k_cat/K_M is the specificity constant comparing enzymes.
depths.deep: k_cat/K_M is bounded by diffusion (~10^8–10^9 M^-1 s^-1); 'catalytically perfect' enzymes reach this limit, linking kinetics back to diffusion physics.

atoms.art_prompt: a saturating rate-vs-substrate hyperbola with Km at half Vmax

quiz.prompt: What does K_M represent on the rate curve?
quiz.answer: The substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate (V_max/2).

quiz.prompt: What assumption yields the Michaelis–Menten form, and what is the specificity constant?
quiz.answer: Steady state for [ES] (d[ES]/dt ≈ 0); specificity constant is k_cat/K_M.

atoms.title: Transition-state theory (Eyring)
atoms.summary: Reaction rate is set by the free-energy barrier to a transition state — the bridge from thermodynamics to kinetics.

depths.eli5: Reactions go as fast as it is easy to climb the hill between start and finish. Taller hill, slower reaction.
depths.core: Eyring's equation relates a rate constant to the activation free energy ΔG‡ of the transition state, with prefactor k_BT/h (~6×10^12 s^-1 at 310 K). It explains why catalysis = lowering the barrier and why rates are exquisitely temperature-sensitive.
depths.deep: An enzyme accelerates a reaction by binding the transition state more tightly than the substrate — Pauling's insight, and the rationale behind transition-state-analog inhibitors.

atoms.art_prompt: a reaction coordinate with a barrier at the transition state, lowered by a catalyst

quiz.prompt: What single quantity sets the rate in transition-state theory?
quiz.answer: The activation free energy ΔG‡ — the barrier height to the transition state.

quiz.prompt: In one sentence, how does an enzyme speed a reaction in this framework?
quiz.answer: By preferentially stabilizing (binding) the transition state, lowering ΔG‡.

atoms.title: Diffusion — Fick's laws
atoms.summary: Matter flows down concentration gradients; the diffusion coefficient D sets how fast.

depths.eli5: Stuff spreads from crowded places to empty ones. The steeper the crowd gradient, the faster the flow.
depths.core: Fick's first law relates flux to the concentration gradient; combined with conservation it gives the diffusion equation ∂c/∂t = D∇²c. Diffusion is how molecules find targets inside cells, and it sets the timescale of unstirred biological transport.
depths.deep: Diffusion is the macroscopic face of random molecular motion — the same D appears in the microscopic mean-square-displacement law (see random walk) and in the Einstein relation.

atoms.art_prompt: molecules streaming down a smooth concentration gradient

quiz.prompt: What does Fick's first law relate?
quiz.answer: Diffusive flux J to the concentration gradient ∇c (J = −D∇c).

quiz.prompt: Write the diffusion equation that follows from Fick's law plus conservation of mass.
quiz.answer: ∂c/∂t = D∇²c.

atoms.title: Einstein–Stokes relation
atoms.summary: Diffusion, temperature, viscosity, and size are linked — bigger and stickier means slower.

depths.eli5: Small things in thin, warm liquid zip around; big things in thick, cold liquid crawl.
depths.core: The Einstein relation D = kT/γ plus Stokes drag γ = 6πηr for a sphere gives D = kT/(6πηr). It lets you estimate a molecule's diffusion coefficient from its size, or its size from a measured D (e.g. dynamic light scattering).
depths.deep: It is a fluctuation–dissipation result: the same friction γ that dissipates motion also sets the magnitude of thermal kicks — random force and drag are two faces of one coin.

atoms.art_prompt: a sphere buffeted by thermal kicks while feeling viscous drag, with D, eta, r labeled

quiz.prompt: How does diffusion coefficient depend on particle radius and viscosity?
quiz.answer: Inversely on both: D = kT/(6πηr) — bigger or more viscous means slower diffusion.

quiz.prompt: From the Einstein relation D = kT/γ and Stokes drag, get D for a sphere.
quiz.answer: Substitute γ = 6πηr: D = kT/(6πηr).

atoms.title: Random walk & mean-square displacement
atoms.summary: Diffusing molecules spread as the square root of time — the microscopic origin of Fick's laws.

depths.eli5: A drunkard's walk covers distance slowly: to go twice as far takes four times as long.
depths.core: For unbiased random motion, mean-square displacement grows linearly in time (⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt in 1D; 6Dt in 3D). The √t scaling is why diffusion is fast over nanometers but hopeless over centimeters — setting the size limit of diffusion-fed cells.
depths.deep: Anomalous diffusion (⟨x²⟩ ~ t^α, α ≠ 1) signals crowding or binding and is a rich readout in single-particle tracking inside cells.

atoms.note: Diffusion time scales as L²/D — estimate it before assuming transport is fast.
atoms.art_prompt: a jagged random-walk trajectory with a growing root-time spread

quiz.prompt: How does mean-square displacement scale with time for normal diffusion?
quiz.answer: Linearly: ⟨x²⟩ ∝ t (so distance grows as √t).

quiz.prompt: If a molecule needs ~1 ms to diffuse across a 1 µm cell, roughly how long to cross a 10 µm cell?
quiz.answer: ~100 ms — time scales as L²/D, so 10× distance is 100× time.

atoms.title: The Nernst potential
atoms.summary: The membrane voltage at which an ion's concentration gradient is exactly balanced by the electric field.

depths.eli5: An ion wants to flow from where it's crowded to where it's not; charge it up enough and the push-back balances it. That balancing voltage is the Nernst potential.
depths.core: At equilibrium for a permeant ion, the electrical and chemical driving forces cancel, giving the Nernst (equilibrium) potential. It sets the 'target' voltage each ion pulls the membrane toward and is the foundation of cellular electrophysiology.
depths.deep: With multiple permeant ions you weight by permeability (Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz) to get the resting potential — but each ion's Nernst potential remains the reference it drives toward.

atoms.note: At 310 K, (RT/F)·ln ≈ 61 mV per decade of concentration ratio (×1/z).
atoms.art_prompt: a membrane with an ion gradient balanced by a voltage, forces canceling

quiz.prompt: What does the Nernst potential represent?
quiz.answer: The membrane voltage at which an ion's chemical gradient is exactly balanced by the electrical force (its equilibrium potential).

quiz.prompt: A 10× outside:inside gradient of a monovalent cation gives roughly what equilibrium potential at body temperature?
quiz.answer: About +61 mV (≈ 61 mV per tenfold ratio for z = +1).

atoms.title: Lipid bilayer self-assembly
atoms.summary: Amphiphilic lipids spontaneously form bilayers — the cell's barrier — driven by the hydrophobic effect.

depths.eli5: Soap-like molecules with a water-loving head and oily tail line up tail-to-tail into a sheet that keeps water out.
depths.core: Because lipids have a polar head and nonpolar tails, burying the tails away from water (hydrophobic effect) drives self-assembly into a bilayer. The result is a fluid, self-healing 2D sheet — the structural basis of all membranes and of compartmentalization.
depths.deep: Molecular shape (packing parameter) selects bilayers vs micelles vs hexagonal phases; bilayer bending and fusion energetics (see Helfrich-type elasticity) govern vesicles, membrane shaping, and pore formation.

atoms.art_prompt: amphiphilic lipids assembling tail-to-tail into a fluid bilayer sheet

quiz.prompt: What drives lipids to form a bilayer?
quiz.answer: The hydrophobic effect — burying the nonpolar tails away from water.

quiz.prompt: Why is a bilayer described as 'self-healing'?
quiz.answer: Exposing tails to water is costly, so the bilayer spontaneously reseals to minimize that exposure.

atoms.title: Hodgkin–Huxley & the action potential
atoms.summary: Voltage-gated ion conductances make the membrane an excitable circuit that fires all-or-none spikes.

depths.eli5: Tiny voltage-controlled gates open and close, letting the cell snap to a spike and reset — the language of neurons.
depths.core: The membrane is a capacitor in parallel with ion-specific conductances. Hodgkin and Huxley described how voltage-dependent Na⁺ and K⁺ conductances (with gating variables) produce the action potential: fast Na⁺ influx depolarizes, slower K⁺ efflux repolarizes. Each current drives V toward that ion's Nernst potential.
depths.deep: It was a quantitative, predictive model fit to voltage-clamp data — a landmark of biophysics — and the gating variables presaged the molecular structure of voltage-gated channels.

atoms.art_prompt: a membrane equivalent circuit with Na and K conductance branches producing a spike

quiz.prompt: Which two ion conductances chiefly generate the classic action potential, and what does each do?
quiz.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ (fast depolarization) and K⁺ (slower repolarization).

quiz.prompt: Why does each ionic current term have the form g_i(V − E_i)?
quiz.answer: It is Ohm's law with E_i the ion's Nernst potential: the driving force is the deviation of V from equilibrium, scaled by conductance g_i.

atoms.title: Elastic network models (GNM/ENM)
atoms.summary: Model a protein as nodes connected by springs; the soft normal modes predict functional flexibility remarkably well.

depths.eli5: Pretend the protein is balls joined by springs. Where it naturally wobbles tells you which parts are floppy.
depths.core: The Gaussian Network Model connects residues within a cutoff by identical springs and diagonalizes the connectivity (Kirchhoff) matrix. Despite its crudeness, the low-frequency modes reproduce experimental B-factors and RMSF — flexibility is largely encoded by the contact topology, not chemical detail.
depths.deep: Because GNM is parameter-free and analytic, it cannot 'leak' homology information — making it a strong, honest baseline against which learned flexibility predictors (e.g. sequence models) should be judged.

atoms.note: A recurring lesson: simple physics baselines (GNM) often match or beat ML for flexibility.
atoms.art_prompt: a protein reduced to a spring network with soft low-frequency modes highlighted

quiz.prompt: What does a Gaussian Network Model represent the protein as, and what do its soft modes predict?
quiz.answer: Residues as nodes joined by identical springs; the low-frequency modes predict flexibility (B-factors / RMSF).

quiz.prompt: Why is GNM a good 'honest' baseline for flexibility prediction?
quiz.answer: It is analytic and trained on nothing, so it cannot exploit homology/data leakage — any learned model must beat it fairly.

atoms.title: Molecular dynamics
atoms.summary: Integrate Newton's equations on a force field to watch biomolecules move atom-by-atom.

depths.eli5: Give every atom a tiny push according to the forces between them, repeat a billion times, and watch the molecule dance.
depths.core: MD numerically integrates F = ma (via the Verlet algorithm) using an empirical force field for bonds, angles, electrostatics, and van der Waals. It yields trajectories from which thermodynamic and kinetic properties are computed — bridging structure and function in motion.
depths.deep: The sampling problem is central: femtosecond timesteps vs millisecond biology means rare events need enhanced sampling (umbrella sampling, metadynamics) or Markov state models to be reachable.

atoms.art_prompt: atoms tracing trajectories under force-field interactions over time

quiz.prompt: What does molecular dynamics integrate, and with what model of the forces?
quiz.answer: Newton's equations of motion (F = ma), using an empirical force field.

quiz.prompt: What is the central limitation of plain MD, and one way around it?
quiz.answer: The timescale/sampling gap (fs steps vs ms events); enhanced sampling or Markov state models help bridge it.

atoms.title: AlphaFold & pLDDT
atoms.summary: Deep learning predicts structure from sequence; pLDDT is its per-residue confidence — often misread as flexibility.

depths.eli5: An AI guesses a protein's shape from its letters and marks how sure it is at each spot. People wrongly treat 'unsure' as 'floppy'.
depths.core: AlphaFold predicts 3D structure from sequence and a multiple-sequence alignment, with pLDDT as a per-residue confidence score. Low-pLDDT regions correlate with disorder/flexibility on average but the score is a confidence, not a physical flexibility — a live 2025 debate.
depths.deep: Conflating pLDDT with dynamics is a leakage/observable-mismatch trap: confidence reflects predictability (including conservation), so honest flexibility benchmarks must compare against physics (GNM) and control for homology.

atoms.art_prompt: a predicted fold colored by per-residue confidence, with a caution flag over low-confidence loops

quiz.prompt: What does pLDDT measure, and what is it NOT?
quiz.answer: It is AlphaFold's per-residue confidence; it is not a direct measure of physical flexibility.

quiz.prompt: Why is using pLDDT as a flexibility predictor risky?
quiz.answer: Confidence reflects predictability/conservation, not dynamics, so it can mislead unless benchmarked against physics and homology-controlled.

atoms.title: Protein language models (ESM)
atoms.summary: Transformers trained on millions of sequences learn representations that predict structure, function, and mutation effects.

depths.eli5: Train an AI on a huge library of protein 'sentences' and it learns the grammar — enough to guess effects of changing a letter.
depths.core: Like language models for text, ESM models are trained by masked-token prediction on protein sequences; their embeddings capture evolutionary and structural signal usable for downstream tasks. But on tasks like flexibility, sequence-only models can underperform simple physics and can hide homology leakage.
depths.deep: Evaluating these models honestly requires fold-disjoint (e.g. CATH-superfamily-disjoint) splits; otherwise apparent skill is partly memorized homology rather than transferable biophysics.

atoms.note: A theme across modern biophysics ML: control for homology leakage or your benchmark lies to you.
atoms.art_prompt: a transformer attending over a protein sequence, embeddings projecting to structure

quiz.prompt: How are protein language models like ESM trained?
quiz.answer: By masked-token prediction over large databases of protein sequences (self-supervised).

quiz.prompt: Why must flexibility/function benchmarks use fold-disjoint splits for these models?
quiz.answer: To prevent homology leakage — without it, apparent skill can be memorized similarity rather than real generalization.

atoms.title: Disordered proteins & phase separation
atoms.summary: Many proteins lack a fixed fold; some demix into liquid droplets that organize the cell without membranes.

depths.eli5: Some proteins are floppy by design, and crowds of them can clump into liquid droplets — like oil drops that sort cell contents.
depths.core: Intrinsically disordered regions sample ensembles rather than one structure. Multivalent weak interactions among them can drive liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming biomolecular condensates that compartmentalize biochemistry without a membrane.
depths.deep: Sequence patterning (charge blocks, aromatic 'stickers') tunes condensate formation; aberrant transitions from liquid to solid are linked to amyloid disease — connecting LLPS to aggregation.

atoms.art_prompt: disordered chains with sticker residues coalescing into a liquid droplet

quiz.prompt: What is a biomolecular condensate, and what drives its formation?
quiz.answer: A membraneless liquid compartment formed by liquid–liquid phase separation, driven by multivalent weak (often disordered) interactions.

quiz.prompt: How can phase separation connect to disease?
quiz.answer: Aberrant liquid-to-solid transitions of condensates can seed pathological aggregation (e.g. amyloid).

atoms.title: Amyloid aggregation & nucleation
atoms.summary: Proteins can misassemble into ordered β-sheet fibrils through a nucleation-and-growth process central to neurodegeneration.

depths.eli5: Sticky protein pieces can lock into long ordered fibers; once a seed forms, more pile on fast — the hallmark of diseases like Alzheimer's.
depths.core: Amyloid formation follows nucleation–elongation kinetics: a slow, unfavorable nucleus forms, then fibrils grow and can self-replicate (secondary nucleation). Aggregation propensity (sequence stickiness), not just fold stability (ΔΔG), often governs which mutations accelerate disease.
depths.deep: Thioflavin-T fluorescence reports the sigmoidal kinetics; for intrinsically disordered amyloid proteins, a folding-stability predictor is the wrong observable — aggregation scales (e.g. AGGRESCAN) match the phenotype better, a clean example of matching method to question.

atoms.note: Match the observable to the question: for disordered amyloid mutants, aggregation propensity beats ΔΔG.
atoms.art_prompt: monomers nucleating into an ordered cross-beta fibril with a sigmoidal growth curve

quiz.prompt: What kinetic process describes amyloid formation?
quiz.answer: Nucleation–elongation (a slow nucleation step followed by rapid fibril growth, often with secondary nucleation).

quiz.prompt: For familial amyloid mutations in a disordered peptide, why might aggregation propensity predict disease better than ΔΔG?
quiz.answer: There is no stable fold to destabilize, so folding ΔΔG is the wrong observable; stickiness/aggregation scales match the actual aggregation phenotype.

atoms.title: MD datasets at scale (mdCATH)
atoms.summary: Large, fold-diverse MD archives enable proteome-scale, leakage-controlled tests of biophysical hypotheses.

depths.eli5: Instead of simulating one protein, use a huge library of simulated proteins to test ideas fairly across all shapes.
depths.core: Datasets like mdCATH provide all-atom trajectories across thousands of CATH domains and temperatures. They let you ask whether a rule (e.g. what unfolds first, or what predicts flexibility) holds across fold space under honest, CATH-superfamily-disjoint splits — turning anecdotes into benchmarks.
depths.deep: A frequent finding: single-domain 'lore' fails to generalize at scale, and simple structural/topological features (contact order, network models) carry most of the transferable signal — a humbling, useful corrective.

atoms.art_prompt: thousands of small protein trajectories tiled into a fold-diverse benchmark grid

quiz.prompt: What does a fold-diverse MD dataset enable that single-protein studies cannot?
quiz.answer: Proteome-scale, homology-controlled (fold-disjoint) tests of whether a biophysical rule generalizes across fold space.

quiz.prompt: Why use a CATH-superfamily-disjoint split when benchmarking on such data?
quiz.answer: To prevent homology leakage, so measured skill reflects genuine generalization rather than memorized fold similarity.
